{"translation_en":null,"larger_context_summary":"Jane speaks to Rochester during their reunion at Ferndean near the novel’s end. Formerly his governess and beloved, she had left after discovering at their interrupted wedding that he was already married. Since then, Thornfield has burned, Rochester’s wife Bertha has died, and Rochester has been blinded and physically disabled while attempting to rescue others. Now independently wealthy, Jane returns by choice. Rochester fears that his injuries and dependence have made him unworthy of her; Jane counters that she values the new reciprocity between them and loves him more, not less, when she can care for him rather than merely receive his protection.","interpretive_commentary":"The statement is principally a considered report of Jane’s emotional state: the comparative “better now … than I did” explicitly treats her love as enduring and intensified across changed circumstances. Its high truth-asserting force is therefore especially natural. The declaration also reassures Rochester and helps reshape their relationship around greater equality and mutual usefulness, but those consequences do not make the words themselves a promise or undertaking; any performative commitment remains limited and context-dependent. Nor is intensity of feeling the same as expressive or reflexive force. Jane’s syntax is controlled, comparative, and explanatory, presenting reasons for how she feels rather than functioning as an involuntary emotional outburst. The avowal is also significant because it rejects Rochester’s fear that disability has diminished his desirability: her present ability to assist him deepens affection without reducing love to pity or obligation."}
